title: If It Happens to You
intro: Learn what to do in the first hour after a scam, why speaking up early matters, and how to spot the second scam that promises to get your money back.
recap: Stop all contact and payments straight away.
Call your bank on the number from your card or its official app, never one from a message.
Keep the evidence: screenshots, numbers, times and amounts. Do not delete the messages.
Be careful of anyone who offers to recover your money for a fee. That is a second scam.
Being scammed does not mean you were foolish. Report it and warn others.

aiTutor.recap: Smart, careful people get scammed. What matters next is acting quickly and calmly, and not being tricked a second time. The first hours are the most useful ones.
aiTutor.example: Ngozi sends 50,000 naira to a fake seller and feels sick. She tells her bank within the hour and saves the chat. Because she acts quickly, the bank has more it can try, and the evidence helps them follow the payment.
aiTutor.watchOut: Embarrassment makes people wait, hoping they were wrong. Waiting only helps the scammer. A quick call that turns out to be unnecessary costs you nothing.
aiTutor.tryThis: Decide now who you would tell first if this happened to you, so you do not have to think when you are upset.

glossary.definition: The feeling of embarrassment or foolishness after something goes wrong. Scammers rely on it, because it keeps victims quiet and slow.
glossary.example: "I am too embarrassed to tell my bank" is the thought a scammer hopes you have.

paragraphs: Scammers are professionals. They do this every day, and they know exactly which feelings to press. Being caught out says nothing bad about your intelligence.
Shame is the scammer's friend. People who stay quiet lose more time, and others get caught by the same trick. Speaking up early is the best thing you can do for yourself and for others.
Next, you will learn what to do in the first hour, and the second scam to watch out for: the one that promises to get your money back.

aiTutor.explain: Tap each step. The order matters, because money is easier to stop the sooner you act. Stop, call, save, report: each step protects the next one.
aiTutor.example: You paid a fake seller and they now ask for a small extra fee. You stop replying, call your bank from the number on your card, screenshot the chat and the transfer, then report the seller's profile to the platform.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not delete the chat or block the number before saving copies. Your bank and the authorities may need that evidence.
aiTutor.tryThis: Write the four words on a note in your phone: stop, call, save, report.

glossary.definition: Anything that shows what happened: screenshots, messages, call times, account numbers and receipts.

nodes.label: 1. Stop
nodes.title: Stop all contact and payments
nodes.definition: Do not reply, do not pay anything more, and do not click further links. Every extra payment is lost money.
nodes.bonusFact: Scammers often ask for "one more small payment" to release the first one. Every extra payment makes the loss bigger, so the safest answer is no.

nodes.label: 2. Call
nodes.title: Call your bank or provider
nodes.definition: Use the number on your card or in its official app, never one from the message. Tell them what happened, and ask them to protect your account and change your PIN or password.
nodes.bonusFact: The sooner a bank hears about it, the more it can try to do.

nodes.label: 3. Save
nodes.title: Save the evidence
nodes.definition: Take screenshots of the messages, the sender's number or profile, and any account details. Write down the times and amounts. Do not delete anything.
nodes.bonusFact: Good evidence helps your bank and the authorities follow what happened.

nodes.label: 4. Report
nodes.title: Report it and warn others
nodes.definition: Report to the police or the proper authority in your area, and to the platform where it happened. Tell family and friends so the same trick does not catch them.
nodes.bonusFact: Reports help others get protected, even when your own money cannot be returned.

widgetData.completionMessage: You now know the four steps for the first hour: stop, call, save, report.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: Save these four words on your phone so you do not have to think when you are upset. Acting in order, even imperfectly, is far better than waiting.

aiTutor.explain: Someone who knows you were scammed and offers a quick fix is a warning sign, not a rescuer. Ask how they could know, and why they want money before they have done anything.
aiTutor.watchOut: Recovery scammers can look professional, with websites and fake case numbers. They always ask for money or details before they help.

widgetData.question: Days after you lose money, a stranger messages: "I can get your money back. Pay a 10,000 naira fee first." What should you do?

options.text: Pay the fee, because it is small compared with what you lost.
Do not pay. It is probably a recovery scam, so report the message.
Send them your bank details so they can start.

widgetData.explanation: Scammers look for people who were already scammed, because they are worried and hopeful. An unknown person who asks for a fee to recover your money is running another advance fee trick.
widgetData.bonusFact: Genuine help comes from your bank and the authorities, and you contact them, not the other way round. If anyone contacts you first, treat it as a risk.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false. Think about what helps you and others, and what only helps the scammer.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each card, ask: does this make it easier or harder for the scammer to get away with it?

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: Telling your bank quickly gives it the best chance to help.
cards.explanation: Time matters. The earlier a bank knows, the more options it may have.
cards.bonusFact: Call the number on the back of your card or on the bank's official site, not one from a message.

cards.statement: You should delete the scam messages so you can forget about it.
cards.explanation: Those messages are evidence. Keep them, and save copies before blocking the sender.
cards.bonusFact: Take screenshots of the messages, numbers and payment details, and keep them somewhere safe.

cards.statement: Being scammed means you were careless or foolish.
cards.explanation: Scams are built by professionals to work on careful people too. Shame only makes it harder to act quickly.
cards.bonusFact: Telling someone you trust early is a strong first step, not a sign of weakness.

cards.statement: Warning your friends and family about the trick can protect them.
cards.explanation: Scammers reuse the same story. One warning can stop the next person.
cards.bonusFact: Even a short message about what happened makes the same trick harder to reuse.

screens.title: Match the Action to Its Reason

aiTutor.review: Match each action to the reason behind it. Each action either stops further loss, gets real help, or protects other people, and knowing the reason makes the steps easy to remember.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not skip steps because the amount was small. The same trick may be used on you again, or on someone you know.

aiTutor.review: One last check. This sentence sums up the whole course: whatever the trick, the defence is to slow down and check another way.
aiTutor.tryThis: Pick one lesson from this course and teach it to a friend or relative this week.

widgetData.template: When money or secrets are asked for, slow down, check another way, and {blank} before you act.
widgetData.explanation: Urgency, fear, greed and trust all work best when you do not stop to think. Checking another way gives you the time, and the time takes the scammer's power away.
widgetData.bonusFact: Sharing what you learned here with one person is the best way to make it stick, and it may protect someone you care about.
